segments.t: We're still in the nineteen eighties, in the same communal flat. Last time, Vanya's father came home from Hungary with gum, markers and a toy car, and told him to share everything; little Arkady only watched. Now Arkady asks Vanya for a piece of gum, and soon the toy car goes missing. We'll hear it in Russian first; don't worry about catching every word.
Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
Let's go through it. The presents have been handed out, and Vanya is enjoying himself in front of Arkady.
'Well, four-eyes?' The word is a schoolyard name for a child in glasses, and it's what Vanya always calls him. Then he shows his empty hands.
'See, there's nothing left.' Literally, 'nothing didn't remain': in Russian, 'nothing' comes with a 'not' as well. Arkady knows that isn't true.
'But you've still got some.' Literally, 'at you there is more'. It's the same pattern as 'I have', just with 'you'. Then he asks.
'Give me just one.' The first word is a command: give. The answer is short.
'No. That's mine.' Remember, his father told him to share with everyone. Arkady has one word for that.
'Greedy!' It's what children shout at someone who won't share. Vanya doesn't care, and shows off his markers.
'See the markers? They're from Japan!' Literally, 'this is Japan', which is how a boy boasts. But then something goes missing.
А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
'Hey, where's the toy car? Where's my toy car?' The word for 'my' ends in an 'a' to match the car, which is feminine. And then Vanya spots Arkady.
'Four-eyes! Grab him!' The verb is the one Dad used when he handed the gum over, 'hold', but here it means 'catch him'. Arkady struggles.
'Let go!' A command again, a short one. Vanya grins.
'Well, well, caught you, didn't we?' One verb in the past tense says it all. Arkady tries to explain.
'I was only looking!' He just wanted to see the car. The verb ends in a plain consonant because Arkady is a boy; a girl would add an 'a'. Vanya has a nasty idea.
Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
'Look, how dirty our toilet is!' The word for 'look' ends in the plural, because he's talking to all the children around him. Then he adds something.

'It needs a wash!' The first word means 'it is necessary', and you'll hear it everywhere. What happens next is cruel: the boys push Arkady's head into the shared toilet bowl. Afterwards, wet and angry, he makes a threat.
'You'll be sorry!' Vanya just laughs at him.
'Oh yeah? When?' The first two words together mean 'oh, really?', said with scorn. And Arkady answers.
Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
'When I grow up, you'll be begging me to forgive you!' Both verbs point to the future: 'when I grow up', and 'you will be asking'. Remember this line, because the whole series is about this promise.
'What did you say?' The verb ends in a plain consonant again, because the 'you' he's asking is Arkady, a boy. Here's the whole scene once more.
Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
That's the promise little Arkady makes, and thirty years later he will get his chance. Next time we jump to the present day, and you'll meet him as the mayor; see you there.
